claim: The zebrafish genome contains two insulin genes – insulin (ins) and insulinb (insb).
source: The zebrafish genome contains two insulin genes – insulin (ins) and insulinb (insb).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the zebrafish genome composition, representing established knowledge about the species.

claim: A 16 bp deletion allele of ins was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis, we generated a 16 bp deletion allele of ins (Figure 1A) and a 10 bp insertion allele of insb.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and described in the methods section.

claim: A 10 bp insertion allele of insb was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis, we generated a 16 bp deletion allele of ins (Figure 1A) and a 10 bp insertion allele of insb.
evidence: This is directly stated as an experimental result from CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis.

claim: ins and insb mutant embryos appear morphologically unaffected.
source: Although ins and insb mutant embryos appear morphologically unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), Insulin was entirely absent in pancreatic islets of ins mutants (Figure 1B), whereas there was no observable change in insb mutant islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This observation is supported by brightfield images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Insulin was entirely absent in pancreatic islets of ins mutants.
source: Although ins and insb mutant embryos appear morphologically unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), Insulin was entirely absent in pancreatic islets of ins mutants (Figure 1B), whereas there was no observable change in insb mutant islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no observable change in insb mutant islets.
source: Although ins and insb mutant embryos appear morphologically unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), Insulin was entirely absent in pancreatic islets of ins mutants (Figure 1B), whereas there was no observable change in insb mutant islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This observation is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: ins mutants exhibit a drastic increase in total glucose levels (up to 10-fold), measured from 1 to 6 days post fertilization (dpf).
source: ins mutants exhibit a drastic increase in total glucose levels (up to 10-fold), measured from 1 to 6 days post fertilization (dpf) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ins mutants show large unused yolk reserves, suggesting defects in lipid absorption and processing.
source: Additionally, staining for lipid content using Nile Red revealed large unused yolk reserves (Figure 1D), suggesting defects in lipid absorption and processing.
evidence: This is based on Nile Red staining data shown in Figure 1D, with an inference about the biological meaning.

claim: ins mutants do not survive beyond 12 dpf.
source: Due to a combination of these metabolic defects, ins mutants do not survive beyond 12 dpf (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 3 month old (adult) ins +/- animals are normoglycemic.
source: Moreover, although 3 month old (adult) ins +/- animals are normoglycemic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), 50 dpf (juvenile) ins +/- animals are noticeably smaller (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), consistent with a role for Insulin in growth control (Nakae et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 50 dpf (juvenile) ins +/- animals are noticeably smaller.
source: Moreover, although 3 month old (adult) ins +/- animals are normoglycemic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), 50 dpf (juvenile) ins +/- animals are noticeably smaller (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), consistent with a role for Insulin in growth control (Nakae et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by body length measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Insulin plays a role in growth control.
source: Moreover, although 3 month old (adult) ins +/- animals are normoglycemic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), 50 dpf (juvenile) ins +/- animals are noticeably smaller (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), consistent with a role for Insulin in growth control (Nakae et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nakae et al., 2001.

claim: insb mutants are viable and fertile.
source: insb mutants, on the other hand, are viable and fertile.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study.

claim: During WT development, insb expression is minimal beyond 48 hpf.
source: During WT development, insb expression is minimal beyond 48 hpf (Papasani et al., 2006; White et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), and it is undetectable in adult β-cells (Tarifeño-Saldivia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: insb is undetectable in adult β-cells.
source: During WT development, insb expression is minimal beyond 48 hpf (Papasani et al., 2006; White et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), and it is undetectable in adult β-cells (Tarifeño-Saldivia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tarifeño-Saldivia et al., 2017.

claim: insb overexpression successfully lowered glucose levels under hyperglycemic conditions resulting from morpholino-mediated ins knockdown.
source: Under the hyperglycemic conditions resulting from morpholino (MO)-mediated ins knockdown, insb overexpression successfully lowered glucose levels, thus indicating that insb is functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: insb is functional.
source: Under the hyperglycemic conditions resulting from morpholino (MO)-mediated ins knockdown, insb overexpression successfully lowered glucose levels, thus indicating that insb is functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of insb overexpression to lower glucose levels.

claim: Survival and metabolic homeostasis in zebrafish depends primarily on ins due to the post-embryonic expression of ins.
source: However, due to the post-embryonic expression of ins, survival and metabolic homeostasis in zebrafish depends primarily on ins.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns and mutant phenotypes described.

claim: The predominant role of ins distinguishes the zebrafish insulins from the redundant metabolic roles of mouse Ins1 and Ins2.
source: This predominant role of ins distinguishes the zebrafish insulins from the redundant metabolic roles of mouse Ins1 and Ins2 (Duvillié et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by a citation to Duvillié et al., 1997.

claim: Mouse Ins1 and Ins2 have redundant metabolic roles.
source: This predominant role of ins distinguishes the zebrafish insulins from the redundant metabolic roles of mouse Ins1 and Ins2 (Duvillié et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duvillié et al., 1997.

claim: Pathways like gluconeogenesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, sirtuin signaling, and oxidative phosphorylation were affected in diabetic conditions across multiple studies.
source: Strikingly, pathways like gluconeogenesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, sirtuin signaling, and oxidative phosphorylation, which were affected in diabetic conditions across these studies, were similarly disrupted in zebrafish ins mutants (Figure 1F and supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of multiple published proteomics studies.

claim: Pathways like gluconeogenesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, sirtuin signaling, and oxidative phosphorylation were similarly disrupted in zebrafish ins mutants.
source: Strikingly, pathways like gluconeogenesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, sirtuin signaling, and oxidative phosphorylation, which were affected in diabetic conditions across these studies, were similarly disrupted in zebrafish ins mutants (Figure 1F and supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 1F and supplementary file 1.

claim: Zebrafish ins is crucial for metabolic homeostasis and survival.
source: Together, these findings indicate that zebrafish ins is crucial for metabolic homeostasis and survival, and that its absence causes core features of diabetic metabolism already at larval stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in ins mutants.

claim: The absence of zebrafish ins causes core features of diabetic metabolism already at larval stages.
source: Together, these findings indicate that zebrafish ins is crucial for metabolic homeostasis and survival, and that its absence causes core features of diabetic metabolism already at larval stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic and phenotypic data presented.

claim: The endoderm transplantation procedure was remarkably efficient at contributing to host endoderm.
source: This transplantation procedure was remarkably efficient at contributing to host endoderm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–A''), and the pancreatic islet of nearly every host embryo contained both donor derived (i.e., ins +/+) as well as host β-cells (Figure 2B–B'').
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–A''.

claim: The pancreatic islet of nearly every host embryo contained both donor derived (i.e., ins +/+) as well as host β-cells.
source: This transplantation procedure was remarkably efficient at contributing to host endoderm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–A''), and the pancreatic islet of nearly every host embryo contained both donor derived (i.e., ins +/+) as well as host β-cells (Figure 2B–B'').
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B–B''.

claim: Genotyping of chimeric animals revealed a near Mendelian ratio of mutant animals.
source: These chimeric animals were raised to adulthood and genotyping (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C) revealed a near Mendelian ratio of mutant animals (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Chimeric animals contain ins +/+ endodermal tissues but retain an ins -/- germline.
source: In summary, these chimeric animals contain ins +/+ endodermal tissues but retain an ins -/- germline, thereby allowing an all-mutant progeny to be obtained by incrossing.
evidence: This is inferred from the transplantation design and genotyping results.

claim: Chimeric animals allow an all-mutant progeny to be obtained by incrossing.
source: In summary, these chimeric animals contain ins +/+ endodermal tissues but retain an ins -/- germline, thereby allowing an all-mutant progeny to be obtained by incrossing.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the germline genotype of the chimeric animals.

claim: Metformin exhibited no glucose-lowering effect in ins mutants.
source: Surprisingly, metformin and MLR1023 exhibited no glucose-lowering effect in ins mutants, suggesting that they act more as sensitizers of insulin signaling rather than independently of insulin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MLR1023 exhibited no glucose-lowering effect in ins mutants.
source: Surprisingly, metformin and MLR1023 exhibited no glucose-lowering effect in ins mutants, suggesting that they act more as sensitizers of insulin signaling rather than independently of insulin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Metformin and MLR1023 act more as sensitizers of insulin signaling rather than independently of insulin.
source: Surprisingly, metformin and MLR1023 exhibited no glucose-lowering effect in ins mutants, suggesting that they act more as sensitizers of insulin signaling rather than independently of insulin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from their lack of effect in ins mutants.

claim: Pck1 levels are higher in ins mutants compared to wild types.
source: In ins mutants, Pck1 levels are higher compared to wild types (Supplementary file 1), suggesting increased gluconeogenesis in the absence of the inhibitory action of insulin.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Higher Pck1 levels in ins mutants suggest increased gluconeogenesis in the absence of the inhibitory action of insulin.
source: In ins mutants, Pck1 levels are higher compared to wild types (Supplementary file 1), suggesting increased gluconeogenesis in the absence of the inhibitory action of insulin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of Pck1 in gluconeogenesis and insulin's inhibitory effect.

claim: The Pck1 inhibitor, 3 MPA, drastically reduced glucose levels in ins mutants.
source: This observation is also supported by the drastic reduction of glucose levels in ins mutants treated with the Pck1 inhibitor, 3 MPA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Metformin has well-known abilities to reduce hepatic gluconeogenesis.
source: Metformin has well-known abilities to reduce hepatic gluconeogenesis, and it also reduces glucose levels in isoprenaline-treated wild-type zebrafish (Gut et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and a citation to Gut et al., 2013.

claim: Metformin reduces glucose levels in isoprenaline-treated wild-type zebrafish.
source: Metformin has well-known abilities to reduce hepatic gluconeogenesis, and it also reduces glucose levels in isoprenaline-treated wild-type zebrafish (Gut et al., 2013).

claim: Metformin's inability to reduce glucose levels in zebrafish ins mutants reveals metformin's dependence on insulin signaling for its action.
source: However, metformin's inability to reduce glucose levels in zebrafish ins mutants reveals metformin's dependence on insulin signaling for its action.

claim: MLR1023's glucose level lowering effects have been proposed to be insulin-dependent.
source: MLR1023's glucose level lowering effects have been proposed to be insulin-dependent (Ochman et al., 2012), and thus, its inability to lower glucose levels in zebrafish ins mutants further suggests the lack of any insulin signaling in these animals.

claim: 2233 molecules were screened in 2 replicates at 10 μM concentration.
source: We screened 2233 molecules in 2 replicates at 10 μM concentration and found three hits (Figure 3C) that reproducibly reduced glucose levels upon retesting with independent chemical stocks and the unmodified standard glucose measurement kit.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the screening methodology.

claim: Three hits were found that reproducibly reduced glucose levels upon retesting with independent chemical stocks and the unmodified standard glucose measurement kit.
source: We screened 2233 molecules in 2 replicates at 10 μM concentration and found three hits (Figure 3C) that reproducibly reduced glucose levels upon retesting with independent chemical stocks and the unmodified standard glucose measurement kit.
evidence: This is supported by screening data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Flutamide is an androgen receptor antagonist.
source: These three hits - flutamide (androgen receptor antagonist), ODQ (soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) inhibitor (Boulton et al., 1995)) and vorinostat (broad HDAC inhibitor (Finnin et al., 1999)) were found, upon retesting multiple times, to reduce glucose levels by 40, 22% and 19%, respectively (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the drug's mechanism of action.

claim: ODQ is a soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) inhibitor.

claim: The three drugs did not prolong the survival of zebrafish ins mutants.

claim: Flutamide caused a dose-dependent decrease in glucose levels in ins mutants.

claim: Treatment with AR antagonists of two types (steroidal and non-steroidal) caused a consistent decrease in glucose levels across all treatments in ins mutants.
source: Second, we treated ins mutants with AR antagonists of two types: (i) steroidal (Cyproterone) and (ii) non-steroidal (nilutamide, hydroxyflutamide, bicalutamide, enzalutamide), and observed a consistent decrease in glucose levels across all treatments, albeit at varying efficiency (Figure 4A), possibly reflecting the different efficacy of these antagonists towards zebrafish AR (Raynaud et al., 1979; Teutsch et al., 1994; Tran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The varying efficiency of glucose reduction by different AR antagonists possibly reflects the different efficacy of these antagonists towards zebrafish AR.
source: Second, we treated ins mutants with AR antagonists of two types: (i) steroidal (Cyproterone) and (ii) non-steroidal (nilutamide, hydroxyflutamide, bicalutamide, enzalutamide), and observed a consistent decrease in glucose levels across all treatments, albeit at varying efficiency (Figure 4A), possibly reflecting the different efficacy of these antagonists towards zebrafish AR (Raynaud et al., 1979; Teutsch et al., 1994; Tran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations about AR antagonist efficacy.

claim: Injection of ar MO into one-cell stage embryos resulted in a reduction of glucose levels in ar MO injected ins mutants.
source: Finally, to modulate AR protein levels, we injected 1 ng of control or ar MO into one-cell stage embryos and observed a reduction of glucose levels in ar MO injected ins mutants (Figure 4B) but not in ar MO injected wild-type animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Injection of ar MO into one-cell stage embryos did not result in a reduction of glucose levels in ar MO injected wild-type animals.
source: Finally, to modulate AR protein levels, we injected 1 ng of control or ar MO into one-cell stage embryos and observed a reduction of glucose levels in ar MO injected ins mutants (Figure 4B) but not in ar MO injected wild-type animals (Figure 4C).

claim: The data support a role, and a benefit, for antagonizing AR specifically in hyperglycemic conditions.
source: These data support a role, and a benefit, for antagonizing AR specifically in hyperglycemic conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of AR antagonism in hyperglycemic vs normoglycemic conditions.

claim: RNA-Seq analyses of 120 hpf ins mutants treated with flutamide or cyproterone revealed 504 and 476 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) compared to vehicle treated mutants, respectively.

claim: Of the DEGs from flutamide and cyproterone treatments, 40 were regulated in parallel (both up or both down) for both AR antagonists tested.

claim: btg2 and insig1 have been reported to play crucial roles in controlling liver gluconeogenesis.

claim: Upon intraperitoneal injections of flutamide in hyperglycemic adult animals, 19% lower fasting plasma glucose levels were observed.

claim: The 19% lower fasting plasma glucose levels observed with flutamide treatment in hyperglycemic adult animals is likely due to reduced hepatic glucose production.

claim: Blood glucose levels are regulated by multiple tissues including the pancreas, muscle, liver, adipocytes, gut and kidney.
source: Blood glucose levels are regulated by multiple tissues including the pancreas, muscle, liver, adipocytes, gut and kidney (Defronzo, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Defronzo, 2009.

claim: Currently, seven classes of antidiabetic drugs exist, of which only three function without increasing circulating insulin levels and only one that definitively functions independently of insulin.
source: Currently, seven classes of antidiabetic drugs exist, of which only three function without increasing circulating insulin levels and only one that definitively functions independently of insulin (Chaudhury et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chaudhury et al., 2017.

claim: Restoring normoglycemia independently of insulin secretion or action could delay disease progression as an improved glycemic status can restore β-cell mass and function.

claim: The zebrafish serves as an excellent platform to study diabetes due to its high fecundity and amenability to chemical screening.
source: Due to its high fecundity and amenability to chemical screening, the zebrafish serves as an excellent platform to study diabetes, and it has been successfully used to study β-cell mass and activity, as well as glucose metabolism (Andersson et al., 2012; Gut et al., 2013; Tsuji et al., 2014; Nath et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; White et al., 2016; Gut et al., 2017; Matsuda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations demonstrating the use of zebrafish in diabetes research.
